html:
The deadliest earthquake on record, which struck Huaxian in Shaanxi, in northwest China, early in the morning of 23 January 1556, under the Ming dynasty.

Its toll was so high because of how people lived. In the loess plateau of the Wei and Yellow River valleys, many families lived in yaodong, homes dug into the soft, wind-blown loess cliffs. The quake brought the cliffs down on people while they slept, and landslides buried whole villages.

The count usually given is 830,000. That number is the fall in people on the official household registers. Modern studies by China's earthquake agency suggest about 100,000 died in the shaking itself, and that the rest of the drop came from people who died of famine and disease after, or who fled the region.

A scholar who survived, Qin Keda, wrote one of the first known pieces of advice on what to do in an earthquake: at the first shock, stay inside and crouch, rather than run out.

The disaster belongs with others on this chart, such as the Tangshan earthquake of 1976, that show how much the human toll depends on housing and density, not only on the size of the quake.
sum: The deadliest earthquake on record, which struck Huaxian in Shaanxi, in northwest China, early in the morning of 23 January 1556, under the Ming dynasty.
